newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels to advance in absence of Zaire peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Rebels to advance in absence of Zaire peace deal.

text.p: Rebels said they would push on towards Zaire's capital while President Mobutu Sese Seko considers rebel chief Laurent Kabila's demand for his immediate resignation.
But in a new blow to the rebel alliance over its handling of Rwandan refugees, the U.N. refugee agency said on Monday 91 refugees were killed in a stampede on a train in rebel-held northeast Zaire.

South Africa's President Nelson Mandela said fresh talks between Mobutu and Kabila would take place within eight to 10 days after they met on a South African ship on Sunday but failed to broker a deal.
Kabila told Reuters his forces, which were reported by residents to be within 100 km (60 miles) of Kinshasa, would move on the capital while Mobutu considered the rebel demand.
Kabila said by telephone from the ship in Congo's port of Pointe Noire: "If we make it to Kinshasa before the eight days then too bad but we cannot wait while he (Mobutu) makes up his mind."
Church sources said the rebels reached their new positions in one day, advancing from their previous forward base at Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from the teeming city of five million people.

A South African official said Mobutu's offer made on the converted icebreakeer SAS Outeniqua to hand over to an elected president was rejected, but mediators would work in the next few days on a way for him to cede power to a transitional authority.
"The understanding is that Mr Kabila will want to lead that transitional authority," said the official, who would not be named but added that the idea was not to humiliate Mobutu.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Monday 91 Rwandan Hutu refugees died in Sunday's stampede on a train bringing refugees from the jungle and called for such evacuations to be suspended.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said three people remained in critical condition and 75 in hospitals from the disaster on the train from Biaro camp to the northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani.
"We have asked (the rebels) for the train evacuation to be stopped immediately while we assess the situation," he added.
The initial toll was put at more than 100 dead by U.N. aid officials who watched in shock as dozens of refugee bodies tumbled out of six open wagons as the train reached Kisangani.
"I think this is one of the most horrifying events I have ever seen in all my years as an aid worker," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, head of UNHCR's Kisangani operation, who was at the station.
Stromberg pressed rebel authorities for more cooperation with aid agencies. "We need to have control of the trains if we are to be responsible for them," he said.

Kabila's Tutsi-dominated rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has already suffered its worst public relations disaster when the refugees were forced to abandon their camps two weeks ago.
The bodies of refugees crushed or suffocated fell from the carriages as their sides were let down to allow other refugees to get off and make their way to a ferry across the Zaire river.

Some rebel sources said the rebel alliance would delay the final push on Kinshasa until it had a force of 10,000 to 12,000 troops near the capital. At an airport in the southeastern capital of Lubumbashi hundreds of rebels boarded planes on Sunday for the frontlines.
Troops from the United States, the former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain were waiting in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals in the event of trouble.

The rebels have won control of about three quarters of Zaire in just seven months and are advancing on several fronts. Kabila's rebellion has all but broken Mobutu's three-decade hold over the mineral rich, but corrupt, state.
